chapter_en: Sorcery Involving the Dead, and Demons

sections.body_en:
The Lord commanded man to cleave to the good and not to let evil penetrate into him, and thus he would live and not die, as it is stated (Bereshit 2:16-17): "And the Lord God commanded the man, saying: Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat. But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat of it, for on the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." However, man sinned; evil penetrated into him and damaged all the systems of his life and all the systems of nature, and as a result it was decreed that he would die. Yet death is for his good and for his rectification, for without it man could not rid himself of the evil and sin that clung to him. The wicked would continue to do evil without limit, and the strong would rule over the weak, tormenting and exploiting them endlessly in order to increase their wealth and satisfy their desires. Now that there is death, these wicked people eventually die and are punished, and goodness and relief spread through the world. Without death, the righteous too would be terribly frustrated with their lives, for "there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin" (Kohelet 7:20), and the sins that clung to them would continue to wrap around them with no ability to free themselves of them and be redeemed. Now that there is death in the world, death separates the soul from the body and consumes the sins that clung to the body, and thereby the soul is freed of its sins. Sometimes this also involves the sufferings of Gehinnom, but in the end the process of purification continues until the soul ascends to Gan Eden and returns to be connected to God as at first. "And the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (Kohelet 12:7). Thus death rectifies the sins of humanity as a whole, and the sins of each person individually, until the rectification of the world is completed, and all the souls of the people who chose good will rise to their destiny at the end of days, to live once again in the renewed body that the Creator will grant them at the Resurrection of the Dead.

Accordingly, despite the terror and the loss, death is not final cessation. The soul returns to the world of souls, while the body, in which death takes place, gradually returns to its dust, and in the course of this, remnants of life still stir within it. However, while a person is alive, the spirit of life, by whose power he is able to engage in settling and rectifying the world, preserves the basic purity of his body. From the moment he dies, the body becomes an 'avi avot ha-tum'a' (the ultimate source of ritual impurity), because it is sealed off from the Divine light, and the remnants of life that still stir within it do not have the power to add goodness. Therefore the body is left without protection, and the forces of impurity, that is, life forces that have been cut off from their root, long to draw strength for themselves from the remnants of life that stir within it, which have themselves also become distant and disconnected from the soul of the person who died; and this is the basis of sorcery (see Zohar I 131a; 220a). Even after all of his flesh has returned to its dust, there still remains upon what is left of his bones the 'havla de-garmei' (the breath of the bones), a faint trace of life, which expresses the eternal kernel within him, from which he will rise to life at the end of days.1

notes_en.en: The Arizal explained (Etz Ḥayim, Sha'ar 22:2): "When a righteous person dies, his NaRaN (nefesh, ruaḥ, neshama) from the aspect of Atzilut ascend to Atzilut, and his neshama of Beri'a ascends to the Upper Gan Eden, and the ruaḥ of Yetzira to the Lower (earthly) Gan Eden, and the nefesh of Asiya remains in the grave. When the flesh decomposes, that nefesh too ascends on high, and there remains that 'breath of the bones' upon those bones that remain in the grave, as mentioned in Parashat Shelaḥ (Zohar III 170a)." It is explained there that the 'havla de-garmei', which is the mental faculties of smallness (moḥin de-katnut) of the 'nefesh of Asiya', and the sparks always remain "in the grave until the time of the resurrection, for since it is the secret of judgements, the kelipot always have a hold on it, and it cannot separate from the body to ascend on high." Furthermore, "all the kelipot take hold only of them, and their main sustenance is from them; this is why the entire Sitra Aḥra is called 'other gods', as is known, and therefore they do not have the power to separate from the kelipot and ascend on high with the nefesh of greatness of Asiya" (Sha'ar Ha-pesukim on I Shmuel, on the verse "And his mother would make him a little robe," I Shmuel 2:19). That is to say, the forces of impurity draw sustenance from those forces that remained in the nefesh, and it is they that prevent the nefesh from ascending fully. For more on the 'havla de-garmei', see Ramḥal's Da'at Tevunot §130, and below at the end of note 3, in the words of Rabbi Tzadok.

sections.body_en:
The sorcerers who grasped the secret of the remnants of life stirring in the dead, instead of letting the dead person return peacefully to his dust and be freed of his sins, exploited the vitality residing in the dead and through it connected themselves to the forces of impurity, in order to know hidden things and future events and to satisfy their evil inclination. They were able to do this because there is no understanding in the faint vitality that stirs in the dead, which is found in the place of impurity and of the decay of sins. Therefore the sorcerers, by the power of their impurity, can connect to its lower aspects and entice it to help them attain wealth, honour and pleasures, which do not add goodness and blessing but rather destroy the world and exploit it in order to satisfy their evil inclination.

There are three types of sorcerers who seek to know hidden things and future events with the help of the dead: the ba'al ov (necromancer), the yid'oni, and the doresh el ha-metim (one who consults the dead), and all of them are forbidden by Torah law, as it is stated (Devarim 18:10-12): "There shall not be found among you … one who consults an ov or a yid'oni, or one who inquires of the dead. For whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord." And all their deeds are in impurity, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:31): "Do not turn to the ovot or to the yid'onim; do not seek them out, to be defiled by them." Impurity means being sealed off and hidden from the Divine light (above, 19:6).

The Sages explained that the more righteously a person conducted himself during his life, the less control sorcerers have over his body after his death. However, in the first year after his passing, since "there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin," the sorcerers can still connect to the lower part of his soul, which rests upon his body in the grave. But afterwards, when the flesh has decomposed, his soul ascends, and those who practise ov have no ability to control him (Shabbat 152b-153a).

Some of the Sages of Israel hold that all the deeds of those who practise ov, like those of other sorcerers, are falsehood (Rav Shmuel ben Ḥofni Gaon, Rambam and others). However, according to most of the Sages of Israel, although it is true that the words of sorcerers are riddled with lies, they do have a certain power to know hidden things and to cast curses with the help of the forces of impurity, which are spiritual forces that have been sealed off from the Divine light and that lead those drawn after them to destruction.2

notes_en.en:
In the first year, while the decomposition of the flesh has not been completed, the entire aspect of the 'nefesh of Asiya' rests upon the body, and therefore sorcerers have the possibility of controlling it (see Shabbat 152b). After the year, generally the 'nefesh of Asiya' ascends, and only the 'havla de-garmei' remains upon the body, and the sorcerers' control over it diminishes. This is similar to what we learned in Rosh Hashana 17a, that the wicked are judged in Gehinnom for twelve months, and only the very wicked, who stretched out their hands against Zevul, the Upper Temple, that is, against the general aim of the honour of Heaven and the rectification of the world, are judged there for all generations (Rosh Hashana 17a; Arukh La-ner and Maharal's Ḥiddushei Aggadot there). Consequently, it is possible to raise them by ov even after many years, as cited in Gittin 56b regarding Bil'am.
The more whole a person is, the more his body is bound to his soul, and consequently the more he is protected from sorcerers. So too it is explained in the Zohar (III 70b) that the angels of destruction have control over the souls of the wicked who have died, whom they enlist to incite in the world, and sorcerers perform sorcery with their help. But they cannot make use of the righteous, "for they are all holy, their bodies are holy, etc." However, since from the sin of Adam and the decree of death upon man, the world fell from its level, and even supremely righteous people cannot rectify their bodies completely, the forces of evil have a certain ability to control the lower part of their soul; and in this way the woman who practised ov succeeded in controlling the 'havla de-garmei' of Shmuel the prophet (Etz Ḥayim 22:2). And even this was only in the year close to his passing, and on account of the honour of Shaul's kingship (Rema of Fano, Ma'amar Olam Katan §4; Moshi'a Ḥosim by Rabbi Moshe David Valle, I Shmuel 28:14).

sections.title_en: The Ba'al Ov and the Yid'oni
sections.body_en:
A ba'al ov is a sorcerer called a 'pitom' (python), who by means of intentions and whispered incantations, and by knocking his arms against one another, would force spirits of the dead to come up through his male organ, and if it was a woman who practised ov, through her female organ. As a result, the image of the dead person would appear as though rising out of the ground, head downward and feet upward, and the voice of the dead person would speak from the armpit or from the joints of the bones of the ba'al ov, and its voice was low, as if rising from the ground. On Shabbat, because of its holiness, it was not possible to raise the dead by ov. If the sorcerer managed to obtain the skull of a dead person, he would place it before him, and thereby he could exert greater control over the spirits of the dead; and when the image of the dead person rose, its head was upward and its feet downward, and he could also raise it on Shabbat (Sanhedrin 65a-b).3

The yid'oni is named after a bird (the yadua) from which the sorcerer would take a bone and place it in his mouth, burn incense, whisper incantations, pronounce adjurations and perform various acts in order to force the spirit of a dead person to connect with him. As a result the sorcerer would lose his senses, as in epilepsy, and the voice of the dead person would speak from his mouth (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:2; Ḥinukh 256).

There is special severity regarding the ba'al ov and the yid'oni, for their punishment is death by stoning, as it is stated (Vayikra 20:27): "A man or a woman who has in them an ov or a yid'oni shall surely be put to death; they shall stone them with stones; their blood is upon them." Even one who turns to a ba'al ov or a yid'oni in order to know future events or hidden things transgresses a Torah prohibition and defiles his soul, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:31): "Do not turn to the ovot or to the yid'onim; do not seek them out, to be defiled by them; I am the Lord your God." For one who seeks guidance through the ways of sorcery and not according to the Torah cuts himself off from Divine providence and seeks to satisfy his needs through ways of cunning in which there is no blessing or rectification. And if he acted according to the guidance of the ba'al ov or the yid'oni, he is liable to lashes for it.

By contrast, the doresh el ha-metim (below, section 6) is liable to lashes and not to death. And one who turns to a doresh el ha-metim does not transgress a negative commandment (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:13-14; Dina De-ḥayei, Lavin 53), but rather neglects the mitzva "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God" (Devarim 18:13; above, 19:12-13).

The special severity of the sins of the ba'al ov and the yid'oni is that they cause great suffering to the souls of the dead, because they use the dead for their own needs. However, the sorcerers could make use only of the souls of sinners who in their lifetimes inclined after impurity, akin to the impurity of sorcery, and this was part of the sufferings of their punishment.4

notes_en.en:
Sanhedrin 65b: "The Rabbis taught: A ba'al ov includes both one who raises [the dead] by his male organ and one who inquires of a skull. What is the difference between them? One who raises by his male organ – [the dead] does not rise in its normal way, and does not rise on Shabbat. One who inquires of a skull – [the dead] rises in its normal way, and rises on Shabbat." Rashi explained: "By his male organ – he raises the dead and seats it upon his male organ." The book Nishmat Ḥayim (3:26) added that a woman who practised ov would raise [the dead] by her female organ (see Tosafot Sanhedrin 65b, s.v. "Ma'aleh"). According to what is known from the books of the ancient peoples, the meaning of the word 'ov' is a pit. In order to raise the dead, those who practised ov would dig a pit, place offerings in it, such as bread, wine and milk, offer a sacrifice and sprinkle its blood into the pit, for they believed that blood was the food most beloved by the dead. Along similar lines the Torah warned: "You shall not eat over the blood; you shall not practise divination nor soothsaying" (Vayikra 19:26), and the commentators explained that the custom of the diviners who foretold the future was to slaughter an animal next to a pit, in the belief that the demons would come to eat the blood and reveal future events to them (Ramban and Rabbeinu Baḥya on Vayikra 19:26). After bringing the offerings and the blood, they would begin a ceremony held at night, in which they asked the spirit of the dead about hidden things and future events. At the end of the ceremony they covered the pit in order to prevent the spirits of the dead from harming people. See further Ramban (Derashat Ha-Ramban, Torat Hashem Temima 3:18), who related how they used to adjure the dead in order to raise it by ov with the help of "banging [of vessels] in the manner of idolatry"; and Sefer Ha-ikarim (3:8) cited him.
Rabbi Tzadok explained that the 'havla de-garmei' that remains upon the bones in the grave is an imprint of the essence of the desire and life force that were in the person, and the sorcerers try to connect to the base desires that were in the person; this is the reason the dead rises from its heels and is revealed through lowly organs, such as the place of the male organ and the armpit, which are places that symbolise desire (Rabbi Tzadok, Dover Tzedek, Aḥarei Mot, §§31-35, pp. 148-152 in the Har Bracha edition; Radbaz 3:642).

Enticing the souls of the dead and capturing them through sorcery in order to reveal hidden things and future events was done not for their benefit and against their will. As Maharḥu (Rabbi Ḥayim Vital) wrote (Etz Ha-da'at Tov, Emor, s.v. "O yirtzeh") in the name of the Zohar, Parashat Shelaḥ, they did this by taking the skull of the dead person, adjuring it with names of impurity and burning incense, and thereby they captured a soul "and defile it with a great impurity like the impurity of idolatry, and compel and subjugate that soul under the Sitra Aḥra, and it tells future events against its will." The commentators explained that raising by ov disturbs the soul from its rest in the World of Truth (Radak, Metzudot and others, on I Shmuel 28:15). This also emerges from the words of the Sages in Ḥagiga 4b, that the dead are terrified when they are raised by ov, lest they are being summoned to judgement. So too it is explained in the book Brit Menuḥa (Path 6, p. 32b; attributed to Rabbi Avraham of Rimon, the Sephardi), that adjuring the dead through the forces of impurity causes it terror.

sections.title_en: King Shaul and the Woman Who Practised Ov
sections.body_en:
After King Shaul sinned and did not heed the voice of Shmuel the prophet to wipe out the Amalekites, the Lord tore the kingdom from him and gave it to David. Instead of accepting the Lord's decree, Shaul pursued David to kill him, and suspected the priests of Nov of supporting David, and ordered them killed. Some time later, "the Philistines gathered their camps for war, to fight against Israel … And Shaul saw the camp of the Philistines, and he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly. And Shaul inquired of the Lord, and the Lord did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets" (I Shmuel 28:1-6). Instead of repenting and praying, and asking the Lord to forgive him and show him his way, he sought to use sorcery in order to ask Shmuel the prophet, who had died that year, how to act (I Shmuel 28:7-22): "Then Shaul said to his servants: Seek out for me a woman who practises ov, that I may go to her and inquire of her." This was a great humiliation for Shaul, for when he was righteous he had fought against the ovot and the yid'onim and wiped them out of the land, and now, when he was not answered by the Lord, he sinned and sought their help. "And his servants said to him: Behold, there is a woman who practises ov at Ein Dor. And Shaul disguised himself and put on other clothes, and he went, and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night; and he said: Divine for me, please, by the ov, and bring up for me the one whom I shall name to you. And the woman said to him: Behold, you know what Shaul has done, how he has cut off the ovot and the yid'oni from the land; why then are you laying a snare for my life, to cause my death? And Shaul swore to her by the Lord, saying: As the Lord lives, no punishment shall befall you for this thing. Then the woman said: Whom shall I bring up for you? And he said: Bring up Shmuel for me. And the woman saw Shmuel, and she cried out with a loud voice; and the woman spoke to Shaul, saying: Why have you deceived me? For you are Shaul!" The Sages said that all the dead would come up by ov with their feet upward, but here Shmuel came up in glorious majesty with his head upward; from this she understood that this was out of honour for the one asking, who was King Shaul, and she was alarmed, for she thought that Shaul was seeking to incriminate her and kill her.

"And the king said to her: Do not be afraid; what did you see? And the woman said to Shaul: I saw a godly being [literally, 'gods'] coming up out of the earth." The Sages said (Tanḥuma, Emor 4) that when a person asks a ba'al ov to bring up a dead person, the ba'al ov himself sees the dead person but does not hear his words, while the one asking hears his words but does not see him. Therefore Shaul turned to the woman who practised ov, "and he said to her: What is his form? And she said: An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe. And Shaul knew that it was Shmuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and prostrated himself." When Shmuel understood that Shaul had called him through a woman who practised ov, he was indignant: "And Shmuel said to Shaul: Why have you disturbed me, to bring me up? And Shaul answered: I am in great distress, for the Philistines are making war against me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, neither by prophets nor by dreams; therefore I have called you, to make known to me what I should do. And Shmuel said: Why then do you ask me, seeing that the Lord has turned away from you … Moreover, the Lord will also deliver Israel with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me; the Lord will also deliver the camp of Israel into the hand of the Philistines." The Sages further explained (Vayikra Rabba 26:7) that Shmuel told him that if he fled or surrendered to the Philistines he would save his life, and if he went out to battle he would fall together with his sons and would merit being with him in his abode in Gan Eden. "Then Shaul immediately fell full length upon the ground, and was very afraid because of the words of Shmuel; and there was no strength in him, for he had eaten no bread all day and all night." A terrible decision stood before him, and no strength was left in him to stand. The woman took pity on Shaul and sought to strengthen him. "And the woman came to Shaul and saw that he was greatly alarmed, and she said to him: Behold, your maidservant has listened to your voice, and I have taken my life in my hand and have listened to your words which you spoke to me. Now therefore, please, you too listen to the voice of your maidservant, and let me set a morsel of bread before you, and eat, so that you may have strength when you go on your way." Shaul strengthened himself, and so that Israel would not surrender to the Philistines, he went out at the head of his soldiers to battle. And although he knew that in this battle he would die together with his sons, he gave up his life heroically for the honour of Israel, and ended his life in repentance. In the merit of his self-sacrifice, although Israel lost that battle, they did not surrender to the Philistines, and in the battles that followed they defeated them (II Shmuel 5:16-25 [?]).

sections.title_en: The Questions Concerning the Raising of Shmuel the Prophet
sections.body_en:
The Sages related (Shabbat 152b) that a certain heretic asked Rabbi Abbahu: You say that "the souls of the righteous are stored away beneath the Throne of Glory"; how, then, was the woman who practised ov able to bring up Shmuel? Rabbi Abbahu answered that during the twelve months after death, while the body still exists in the grave, the soul of the righteous too still ascends and descends. Only afterwards does the power of the body cease, and the soul ascends and does not descend, and then it can no longer be brought up by ov. The masters of the esoteric teachings added and explained that only the 'havla de-garmei' of Shmuel came up, that is, only a faint radiance of Shmuel's soul, which remained like a breath upon his bones, came up by ov; and even that faint radiance was illuminated by Shmuel's soul so that it would not be defiled by the sorcery.

As we learned (section 2), some of the Sages of Israel hold that all the deeds of those who practise ov and of other sorcerers are falsehood. According to their view, the woman who practised ov knew how to speak in a low voice imitating the voice of a dead person, and thus she deceived Shaul (Rav Shmuel ben Ḥofni Gaon). Others say that indeed those who practise ov generally lied, but here the Lord granted the woman who practised ov the ability to bring up the soul of Shmuel so that it would be revealed to Shaul, and that is why the woman cried out (Rav Sa'adia Gaon and Rav Hai Gaon).

The view of most of the Sages and commentators is that sorcerers have the power to bring up the lower part of the souls of the dead, but when the woman who practised ov tried to bring up Shmuel's soul, by the power of his holiness his soul illuminated the lower part of his soul, and therefore his words were correct, as if he were alive (see Otzar Ha-ge'onim, Ḥagiga, Responsa 2; Radak, I Shmuel 28:24; Radbaz 3:642).5

notes_en.en:
As we learned in note 1, the Arizal explained that those who practise ov bring up the lower part of the soul of the dead, the aspect of the 'havla de-garmei', which remains upon what is left of the bones of the dead until the time of the resurrection. "From this it will be clear to you that that woman who practised ov did not bring up Shmuel, neither in the aspect of neshama, nor in the aspect of ruaḥ, nor in the aspect of nefesh, God forbid, but only that aspect which we call 'the breath of the bones', which is the nefesh of smallness of the World of Asiya" (Sha'ar Ma'amarei Rashbi, Shelaḥ; Etz Ḥayim 22:2), "… for the kelipot always take hold of it, and they have the power to take hold of it …" (Sha'ar Ha-pesukim on I Shmuel, on the verse "And a little robe," I Shmuel 2:19).
The Sages said (Ḥagiga 4b) that when the woman who practised ov called Shmuel the prophet, he thought he was being called to stand in judgement, and he asked that Moshe our teacher come up with him to testify that he had fulfilled the whole Torah. Therefore the woman said: "I saw gods coming up out of the earth" – in the plural: Moshe and Shmuel. Radbaz, in Metzudat David 47, explained that in order that the woman who practised ov should not gain control over Shmuel's soul, the Lord told his ruaḥ and his neshama to return and rest upon his body in the grave, for it was better that he suffer a little thereby than that his body be defiled by the sorcery of the woman who practised ov. So he also wrote in Responsa Radbaz 3:642. In Akedat Yitzḥak (Vayikra, Sha'ar 65), he explained that Shaul knew that the woman who practised ov would not succeed in defiling Shmuel, but he thought that by virtue of her appeal, Shmuel would reveal himself to him in a good manner. In Ha'amek Davar (Devarim 18:14) he explained that in such a situation of danger to life, and in the absence of an answer from a prophet, Shaul was permitted to turn to the woman who practised ov. End of quote.
After all, Shaul sinned when he consulted the woman who practised ov, and this is one of the reasons for his death, as it is stated (I Divrei Ha-yamim 10:13-14): "So Shaul died for his trespass which he committed against the Lord, because of the word of the Lord which he did not keep, and also for asking of an ov, to inquire of it, and he did not inquire of the Lord; therefore He slew him, and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Yishai." So too in Vayikra Rabba 26:7. The Sages further said (Devarim Rabba, Lieberman edition, Va-etḥanan) that the answer he received harmed him, for in truth he could have repented and prayed to the Lord and been saved, but since he learned from Shmuel that he would die, he despaired and died. However, since he gave up his life for Kiddush Hashem, he merited being counted among the righteous. (Some say that this woman who practised ov was a righteous woman, the mother of Avner son of Ner, and she did not actually engage in this, but knew how one raises by ov, just as the Sages of Israel knew how sorcery is performed. Since there was then a great need, they turned to her, and she agreed to take her life in her hands for this purpose, but she did not know that the one turning to her was the king himself. See Akedat Yitzḥak, Sha'ar 65; Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer 33.)

sections.body_en:
Unlike the ba'al ov and the yid'oni, who bring up the dead from their graves and force them to make their voices heard, the doresh el ha-metim connects with the dead while they are still in the grave, and without their voice being heard, their answer is received in his consciousness in a dream (Rambam, Meiri and Radbaz). Some say that receiving answers from them while awake is also included in the prohibition (Semag).

One of the well-known methods of the doresh el ha-metim was to starve himself and spend the night in the cemetery so that a spirit of impurity would rest upon him (Sanhedrin 65b). That is to say, by starving and sleeping in the cemetery at night he would diminish himself, and thus, as he emptied himself of his personal life, he would draw close to the dead and bring upon himself the spirit of impurity within them, and thereby the dead would reveal hidden things to him. There were additional methods of consulting the dead that did not depend on starving or on being in the cemetery, such as wearing special clothing, whispering incantations or burning incense. The general rule is: anyone who does something so that the dead will reveal hidden things to him transgresses the prohibition of "one who inquires of the dead" and is liable to lashes.6

Some say that the prohibition is to inquire of the body of the dead person by means of sorcery, but it is permitted to turn to his spirit, and even to adjure it to reveal hidden things to him, for the spirit of the dead person did not die and is therefore not included in 'the dead' itself. Thus we learned (Berakhot 18b) about Amoraim who turned to the spirits of the dead with a question and received an answer from them (Yere'im; Hagahot Maimoniyot; Rema 179:14). According to this view, those who inquire of the body of the dead cleave to the forces of impurity bound up with the body of the dead, since there was a soul in it, and after it departed, the forces of impurity strive to draw from it the remnants of vitality left there. But when the inquiry is directed to his spirit, there is no impurity in it and it is permitted. And even this is on condition that the inquiry to the spirit is done through speech, or even through adjuration, but not through acts resembling sorcery (Levush 179:14).

On the other hand, some say that the Torah prohibition of inquiring of the dead also includes a prohibition of turning to the spirit of the dead. Anyone who turns to his spirit by means of acts is liable to lashes, and if he did so through words or adjurations, since he did not perform an act, although he transgressed a Torah prohibition he is exempt from lashes (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 13:11 [?]; Beit Yosef 179:14). According to this view, the incidents related in the Gemara (Berakhot 18b) about dead people who revealed themselves to living people took place in a dream, without their having asked the dead to reveal themselves to them. Rather, they prayed to the Lord and asked that the answer be revealed to them, and following this they dreamed that the dead person revealed himself to them and answered their question.

Many have the custom of praying at the graves of the righteous, just as Calev son of Yefuneh prayed at the graves of the Patriarchs that he be saved from the counsel of the spies (Sota 34b). This does not involve the prohibition of consulting the dead, since the prayer is to the Lord. Some are lenient to turn to the souls of the righteous, since the intention is that they will entreat the Lord on their behalf. And although the lenient have something to rely on, it is proper to take the view of the stringent into account.7

notes_en.en: The Yere'im (334-335) wrote that "the ba'al ov brings him up from his grave," whereas the doresh el ha-metim "inquires of him while he is still in his grave"; and so wrote Recanati 566. According to Radbaz in Metzudat David 64, "the ba'al ov is while awake, and this one is in a dream; the ba'al ov is by means of a demon, and this one is by means of adjuring the dead; and therefore the ba'al ov is [punished] by death, and this one by a [mere] warning." However, according to the Semag (Lavin 56), the ba'al ov also transgresses the prohibition of 'one who inquires of the dead'; thus in his view the prohibition of 'one who inquires of the dead' also applies when the dead reveals himself to him while he is awake. Many copied his view, among them Baḥ 179:14 and Dina De-ḥayei (on the Semag there). By whatever method a person tries to connect with the dead, he transgresses the Torah prohibition, and the Sages mentioned the well-known method of one who "starves himself and goes and spends the night in the cemetery" (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:13; Ḥinukh 515:1; Ramban and Rabbeinu Baḥya, Devarim 18:11). Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (Toldot Adam Ve-ḥava 17:5) wrote that it is forbidden to ask the dead even by means of adjuration, and the implication is even without an act (so Beit Yosef 179:14 explained).

In Berakhot 18b it is related that Ze'iri deposited money with his landlady, with whom he was lodging, and after she died he went to the cemetery to ascertain from her spirit where the money was. Likewise Shmuel asked his father, after he died, where he had hidden the money that orphans had deposited with him. From this Rabbi Eliezer of Metz (Yere'im 334-335) learned that only inquiring of the body of the dead is forbidden, but inquiring of his spirit is permitted, "for the spirit is not called dead." So wrote many: Recanati 566; Hagahot Maimoniyot, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:8; Rema YD 179:14; Gra 24; Shiyurei Berakha 7; Binyan Tziyon 67; Maharam Schick OḤ 293; 67 [?]; Sdei Ḥemed (Asifat Dinim, Ma'arekhet Rosh Hashana 1:6), and others. The explanation of the Levush (179:14) cited above is brought in the Shakh there 16; Shulḥan Gavoha 27, and others. So too it is related of the Arizal that he used to connect with the souls of the dead and ask them questions and doubts (Sha'ar Ha-gilgulim, Introduction 38; Ha-Ari Ve-gurav, first letter, p. 8. See also Keter Rosh, Ma'amarim U-ma'asiyot 16, that Rabbi Ḥayim of Volozhin too asked a dead person to reveal himself to him and resolve doubts for him in his learning).
In Beit Yosef 179:14, he wondered at and challenged the Yere'im, and explained that the Amoraim who asked the dead perhaps acted by means of holy names, and that the prohibition of consulting the dead applies only through an act. But in his conclusion he brought the view of Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (Toldot Adam Ve-ḥava 17:5), that it is forbidden to ask a dead person even by means of adjuration without performing an act, and he did not distinguish between the spirit of the dead and his body. The view of the Beit Yosef emerges from the Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:13), the Ḥinukh (515) and the Meiri (Sanhedrin 65b), who wrote that any act or speech that causes the dead to be revealed is included in the prohibition, and they did not distinguish between inquiring of the spirit of the dead or of his body (see Da'at Kohen 69). This also emerges from the view of Radbaz (Metzudat David 64), cited in the next section. (According to this view, the Amoraim received an answer from the dead in a dream without having turned to them; and so explained Rabbi Ya'akov ibn Ḥaviv in Ein Ya'akov; Maharsha, Tzlaḥ and Ben Yehoyada on Berakhot there; and so wrote Rav Nathanson in Divrei Sha'ul, YD 369; and so too in the Derashot of Rabbi Yehoshua ibn Shu'eib for Rosh Hashana.)
Turning to the dead at the graves of the righteous: Many have the custom of praying at the graves of the righteous and asking them to pray for the living. So wrote Sefer Ḥasidim (450); Ḥemdat Yamim (7, pp. 683-684); Ma'avar Yabbok, Siftei Renanot 24; Paḥad Yitzḥak (entry 'Tzrakhav', 49a-b); Yafeh La-lev (II 605:3); Yabi'a Omer IV YD 35:6, and others. On the other hand, according to many one should not turn to the dead at all, but rather turn to the Lord that He accept our prayers in the merit of the soul of the righteous person. So wrote Maharil (Hilkhot Ta'anit 18); Eliyahu Rabba (581:39); Ḥokhmat Adam (89:7); Mateh Efrayim (OḤ 581:50); Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh (128:13); MB (581:27), and others. The Baḥ (YD 217:48) wrote in the name of Rabbi Ḥayim Paltiel that those who vow to go to the cemetery to pray there – "it would appear somewhat like consulting the dead," and he explained that what Ḥazal said, that Calev prayed at the graves of the Patriarchs, means that "he prayed there in a place of holiness, so that his prayer would be heard." However, on the other hand, the Baḥ there noted that "they have already adopted this custom and no one protests, and there is support for it in the Zohar." In practice, it is good to be stringent ab initio, and one who is lenient to turn to the soul of the righteous person to entreat the Lord on his behalf has something to rely on (Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 15:21, note 15).

sections.title_en: Asking a Living Person to Appear in a Dream After His Passing
sections.body_en:
It is related in the Talmud (Mo'ed Katan 28a) that when Rav Naḥman was dying, his disciple Rava sat before him. Rav Naḥman asked Rava to intercede with the Angel of Death that he not cause him suffering at the time of death. Rava answered his teacher: But you, Master, are an 'important person', and presumably the Angel of Death will take your request into greater consideration. Rav Naḥman answered that the one departing is not important before the Angel of Death. Rava prayed for him and asked Rav Naḥman to appear to him after his death. When he appeared to him after his death in a dream, Rava asked him whether he had suffered pain in his death, and he answered that his death was as easy "as removing a hair from milk." But he added that the dread of death was severe, and therefore, if the Holy One, blessed be He, were to offer him to return again to this world, he would not want to, so as not to go through this dread again.

When Rava's own day to die arrived, he too was very afraid that the Angel of Death would cause him suffering, and he asked his brother Rav Se'orim to influence the Angel of Death not to cause him suffering. Rav Se'orim answered him: But your influence over him is greater; why do you not ask yourself? Rava answered: Since I have been handed over to death, he no longer takes me into consideration. Rav Se'orim prayed for him and asked Rava to reveal himself to him after his passing. When he revealed himself to him in a dream, he asked him whether he had suffered pain in his death, and he answered that the pain was as slight as the pain of the scratch of bloodletting.

From this we learn that it is permitted for a person to ask a living person to reveal himself to him in a dream after his death in order to inform him of hidden things (SA 179:14).8

notes_en.en: I have presented the stories with some added interpretation, including that the revelation after death was in a dream, as Rashi and virtually all the commentators wrote. The Shulḥan Arukh (179:14) wrote: "To adjure a sick person to return to him after death to tell him what he will ask him – is permitted." The Beit Yosef explained that this does not involve the prohibition of consulting the dead, since he adjures him during his lifetime. According to Radbaz (Metzudat David 64) this too is forbidden, for anyone who adjures a person to reveal himself to him after death "burdens the soul of the dead – whether good or bad – to come and tell him, when he has already departed from the world." Furthermore, the angel appointed over the souls of the dead is called 'Duma', and "by means of his adjurations he compels the aforementioned angel to grant permission to the soul of the dead to come and answer his question; thus he alters the function of this angel." But he did not write that it is forbidden to ask without an adjuration. And indeed, from the plain sense of the Gemara in Mo'ed Katan 28a, it appears that it was a request and not an adjuration.

sections.body_en:
Included in the prohibition of 'one who inquires of the dead', it is forbidden to conduct a séance, in which the participants imagine that the spirit of a dead person rises and answers their questions by moving a glass on a table on which there are letters. Likewise, any ceremony intended to make contact with the spirits of the dead is included in the prohibition of 'one who inquires of the dead'. As the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:13): "The general rule is: anyone who acts so that the dead will come and inform him receives lashes, as it is stated: 'There shall not be found among you one who makes … pass, etc., or one who inquires of the dead.'" Even according to those who hold that the prohibition of consulting the dead applies to one who inquires of the dead person himself and not to one who connects with his spirit (Yere'im, above, section 6), the intention is that one may connect with the spirit of the dead by means of a request or an adjuration, but it is forbidden to perform an act for this purpose. And the act performed in a séance is included in the forbidden forms of sorcery.9

Regarding channelling with the dead without any particular act (spiritism): There was a rabbi in Romania, Rabbi Ḥayim Falik, who without any act knew how to communicate with the souls of the dead, and he could tell a person that his father in the World of Truth was greatly distressed that he was desecrating Shabbat; and to prove that his father had indeed told him so, he was able to tell him things that only the father and son knew, and thereby he would strengthen him to observe the mitzvot. However, the question arose for him whether this was permitted and proper, and he sent his question to our master Rav Kook. Rav Kook answered that according to the Rambam it is forbidden in any case to turn to the dead, but according to the author of the 'Yere'im' it is permitted to turn to their spirit. However, there is concern that this connection is not with the spirit of the dead person but with a certain part of the soul that rests in the body of the dead, and then even according to the 'Yere'im' it is forbidden. He also raised a remote concern that this might be included in the prohibition of 'raising by ov', since today we do not know all the methods of those who practised ov. After all this, he did not rule decisively that it is forbidden, but concluded: "It is not worthwhile to strengthen faith by such devices, which are close to the stumbling block of prohibition. It is better to fulfil 'You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God'" (Da'at Kohen YD 69).

To summarise: those who communicate with the souls of the dead using a particular object, such as a glass or a ring or anything similar, transgress the prohibition of consulting the dead. If they do not use a particular object, the poskim disagree whether they transgress a Torah prohibition. But even according to those who hold that there is no prohibition in this, it is proper not to turn to them.

Those who communicate with entities that are not the dead, or to whom the souls of the dead reveal themselves without their making any effort to that end, although there is no prohibition in this, it is not advisable for them or for others to rely on the information they received from them. For although there is sometimes truth in this information, it also contains many delusions, and it is difficult to distinguish between the truth and the falsehood in it; and sometimes, specifically in the most important and fateful matter, those revelations falsify or even lie, and the damage from this is great, as we shall learn regarding demons (below, sections 9-10). Indeed, the purer the faith of those who channel, and the better and more refined their character traits, the cleaner their revelations will be. Nevertheless, even if they have found several times that their revelations were true, it is not advisable for them or for others to rely on these revelations as complete truth, but rather as a direction one may consider and draw inspiration from (see above, 17:5-6).

notes_en.en: Séance ceremonies developed about two hundred years ago in the United States and in England. Rabbi Shlomo Kluger (Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, third edition, 2:48) wrote that it is forbidden as kosem (divination) or as sorcery. Likewise Rav Tabak (Teshurat Shai, second edition, 129) answered regarding a Jew who would immerse and recite a chapter of Tehillim before the ceremony, and answered that according to the Rambam and those who follow him it is forbidden, and even according to the other poskim it seems to be forbidden as kosem or as sorcery. He further added that one who engages in this endangers his life, as cited in the Beit Yosef and the Rema 179:16. Rav Ḥayim David Halevi was asked whether it is possible to make use of a gentile who would conduct a séance in order to solve a murder. He answered that even to ask a gentile is forbidden by rabbinic law. He further added that he does not believe that a séance has the power to help (Mayim Ḥayim 2:49; Aseh Lekha Rav 5:69). He further wrote (ibid. 8:51) that one may not transgress this prohibition in order to bring people back to observance. In addition, proof of the survival of the soul does not help bring people to repentance, for in the distant past everyone believed in it, and nevertheless many sinned with idolatry and all the other transgressions.

sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Ḥagiga 16a) that demons are creatures in an intermediate state between the spiritual and the physical, between angels and human beings. In three things they resemble the ministering angels: they have wings, they fly from one end of the world to the other, and they hear from behind the curtain what is going to happen. In three things they resemble human beings: they eat and drink, they are fruitful and multiply, and they die. Among the demons too there are males and females, and the females are called 'ruḥot' (spirits) or 'lilin'. However, the descriptions of the Sages regarding demons are not to be taken literally; rather, they are intended to explain their essence as it appears to people in imagination and in intellect. As the Maharal wrote (Ḥiddushei Aggadot, Gittin 68a), when they say, for example, that demons eat and drink, the Sages' intention is that demons need to receive abundance (shefa) in order to exist.

Some of the Sages of Israel interpret all the words of the Sages about demons as a parable for coarse people whose moral development has not been completed, and who are consequently harmful.

However, according to most of the Sages of Israel, demons are unrectified spiritual forces that are connected to the dark side of man, the side that has not yet been completed: the other side, called in Aramaic 'Sitra Aḥra', as opposed to the side of holiness, which expresses the part whose work has been completed. As an expression of this, the Sages said that demons were created at 'twilight' of the sixth day of Creation, and when Shabbat began their creation had not yet been completed, and man must contend with these incomplete forces and thereby be a partner in the rectification of the world (Avot 5:6; Bereshit Rabba 7:5; Zohar I 14a). The sin of Adam took place on the sixth day, and as a result, at 'twilight' the demons were created, which are deficient forces connected to desolate and dangerous places such as the desert, ruins and desolate roads, as well as to the dark time, the night, and from there they draw harm to those who come into contact with them. After the roots of the demons were created at the 'twilight' preceding the Shabbat of Creation, demons continued to be formed from the sins of man. For sins stem from abundance that was meant to add goodness, but man did not succeed in absorbing it, and thus that abundance turned into external forces that harm man (see Eruvin 18b; Zohar I 19b; 55a).

Among demons there are levels. Corresponding to good people, there are demons that tend to do good, and they are called 'Jewish demons', at whose head is Ashmedai, who the Sages said helped Shlomo in building the Temple. We also find demons who volunteered to help the Sages. Even so, since they express the dark side of man, harm is caused even by demons that tend to do good (see Gittin 68a-b; Zohar III 253a).

Since demons are creatures that express ideas that have begun to be clarified but have not been completed, as the years pass, more ideas are clarified, more desolate places are settled, and more things are rectified, and correspondingly the demons gradually diminish (below, sections 11-12).10

notes_en.en:
Bereshit Rabba 7:5: "'And God said: Let the earth bring forth, etc.' … These are the demons, whose souls the Holy One, blessed be He, created, and when He came to create their bodies – He sanctified the Shabbat and did not create them" (see Mishna Avot 5:6). The Zohar (I 14a) asks: could the Holy One, blessed be He, not have delayed sanctifying the day until after He created bodies for those spirits? Rather, following the sin, the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil aroused the 'Sitra Aḥra', and evil sought to prevail in the world, and evil spirits emerged from it that wanted to strengthen themselves by clothing themselves in bodies. When the Holy One, blessed be He, saw this, He aroused the Tree of Life and the good side, and sanctified the Shabbat day. End of quote. After the completion of Creation, demons are also formed from nocturnal emissions, as the Sages said of Adam, that after he sinned and separated from his wife, "all those years that Adam was under a ban, he begot spirits, demons and lilin" (Eruvin 18b). It is explained in the Zohar (I 19b; III 76b, and elsewhere) that it is the harmful spirits that cause this (in the sense of 'one transgression brings another'). It seems that nocturnal emission is an expression of all the sins of forces that do not reach actual realisation, and from all of them harmful beings are created (see Sha'ar Ha-pesukim, Iyov 15, that from every transgression a destroying angel is created; and likewise Alshikh, Shemot 30, that from a transgression a destroyer is created; and likewise Maharsha on Sota 3b; Nefesh Ha-ḥayim 1:13; Likutei Moharan 22. Tzidkat Ha-tzaddik 162 wrote that more destroyers are created from wasteful emission of seed). For more on demons see Berakhot 6a; Pesaḥim 110a; 112b; Ḥullin 105b. See Zohar III 253a; Shelah, Tractate Shevuot, Ner Mitzva, regarding demons that stem from the side of wisdom (Jewish demons) and demons that stem from the side of desire (gentile demons).
Ramban wrote (Vayikra 17:7): "They are called 'shedim' (demons) because their dwelling is in a place that is laid waste (shadud), such as the desert." Since they are more spiritual, they know future events in the short term. People would sacrifice to them in order to receive information from them, as it is stated (Devarim 32:17): "They sacrificed to demons, not to God, to gods whom they did not know." Involvement with demons defiles, and the prohibition of eating blood and the mitzva of covering the blood are connected to this, because spilled blood expresses vitality that was not realised, similar to demons. Sorcerers would offer blood to demons so that they would reveal future events and hidden things to them, and perform deeds on their behalf, and turn people's hearts to love or to hate (Rabbi Ya'akov Sikili, Torat Ha-minḥa 48; Sod Razaya, Hilkhot Mal'akhim; Derashot of Rabbi Yehoshua ibn Shu'eib, Aḥarei Mot and Kedoshim, where he explained that only on Yom Kippur is a gift given to Azazel, and even then the one who sends away the goat becomes impure and must purify himself). The Sages said (Zohar III 251b) that the mezuza, which expresses faith in the Lord and on which is the name Shaddai, protects the homes of Israel from the harm of demons.
According to the Rambam in the Guide for the Perplexed (1:7), the intention of the Sages in saying that before Adam rectified his sin he begot demons and spirits is that he begot unrectified children, evil and harmful, who did not express the image of God. So wrote Abarbanel, Bereshit 5; Sforno, Ma'amar Kavvanot Ha-Torah; Radak, Bereshit 5:3, in the name of Rav Nissim Gaon in the name of Rav Sherira Gaon; Rashbatz, Magen Avot III:4.

sections.body_en:
Sorcerers would also make use of demons, and anyone who tries to activate demons by means of various acts, such as burning incense, banging on vessels and collecting blood, so that they will perform various actions or reveal hidden things, transgresses the prohibition of "ḥover ḥaver" (one who casts spells) and is liable to lashes (see above, 19:10). One who burns incense to a demon in order to connect with a dead person is liable to stoning like a ba'al ov. And one who burns incense to a demon and accepts it upon himself as a god is liable to stoning like one who worships idolatry (Piskei Rid; Ri'az, Kuntres Ha-re'ayot, Sanhedrin 65a, based on the Gemara there and Keritot 3b).

The Maharal explained that by means of demons it is possible to perform actions similar to sorcery, but demons do not have the power to change the order of the world, only to affect things within reality. By contrast, sorcery changes the order of the world, and therefore the Sages said that sorcerers "contradict the heavenly entourage"; though the effect of sorcery too is only temporary (Ḥiddushei Aggadot, Sanhedrin 67a).

Some say that it is forbidden to activate demons only by means of an act, but it is permitted to activate them by speech. Others say that it is forbidden to activate them even by speech. In practice, since this is a doubt regarding a Torah prohibition, it is forbidden to activate demons by speech (SA 179:16).

However, there is no prohibition in asking demons to reveal hidden things, such as asking them to make known who stole some object and where it is located, or what the cure for a certain sick person is, since one is not asking them to perform an act. However, those who do so come to harm, because demons lie and provoke those who deal with them. Therefore in practice, because of the danger involved, one should not ask demons to reveal hidden things. So too Sefer Ḥasidim (204) wrote that if one sees a person who converted to another religion not because of lust for a woman or for money, "know that he or his forefathers engaged in adjurations and dealings with demons, and permission was given to lead him astray, and punishment is exacted from the father who caused it." It further wrote (206) that sometimes demons mock those who use them, for example by telling them to announce that the Messiah is about to come, and they become a source of shame and disgrace in the eyes of all.

Nevertheless, there were Sages who made use of demons, sometimes for lack of choice (see Me'ila 17b), and sometimes by choice, and apparently they knew that these were demons that tended toward good. But after all, there is danger in this as well, and therefore the masters of the esoteric teachings warned that it is better for a person not to make use of demons at all.11

notes_en.en:
Some say that it is forbidden to activate demons by speech, because this too is included in the prohibitions of sorcery. This is the view of Yad Ramah and Rid on Sanhedrin 67b; Piskei Ri'az 7:4; Meiri there; Ha-ikarim 3:8; Radbaz 3:405. On the other hand, some say that only activating angels of destruction by speech is forbidden as sorcery, but it is permitted to activate demons by speech. For the Sages said (Sanhedrin 67b): "'Be-lateihem' – this is the work of demons; 'be-lahateihem' – this is the work of sorcery," which shows that the work of demons is not included in the forbidden forms of sorcery. So wrote Ramban (Responsa attributed to him, 283), Rashba (1:413) and Semag (Lavin 55), and the Rosh (Sanhedrin 7:8) inclined to this view. As halakha, SA 179:16 ruled stringently.
Sanhedrin 101a: "One may not consult demons on Shabbat (because it is a weekday activity). Rabbi Yosi says: Even on a weekday it is forbidden," because of danger. But Rabbi Yosi too agrees that there is no prohibition of sorcery in asking a demon about hidden things (Rosh there 7:8). So too it was ruled in SA (OḤ 307:18) that it is permitted on Shabbat to ask a demon how to heal a sick person (Magen Avraham 301:26; MB 307:67). When it is not for the needs of a sick person, it is forbidden on Shabbat as a weekday activity. So wrote the Maharal (Be'er Ha-gola, Second Well, p. 29) and Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (307:32). Some disagree and hold that it is forbidden to consult demons (Ḥasdei David on Tosefta Shabbat 8:11; Shulḥan Gavoha YD 179:29). In their view, this is what the Shulḥan Arukh ruled in YD 179:16. Perhaps their view is based on a different reading in the Gemara in Sanhedrin (see Gra 179:26).
Some say that the dispute over whether it is permitted to activate demons to perform an act by speech refers to the words of an incantation, but to adjure them by holy names to perform an act is permitted according to all opinions, since it is done out of the holiness of the Name (Yere'im 239; Rabbeinu Yeruḥam; Rema 179:16). But they too agree that any involvement with demons is dangerous, as the Beit Yosef wrote, and the Rema cited it (179:16): "Nevertheless, most of those who engage in this do not take leave of them in peace; therefore one who guards his soul will keep far from them."

sections.title_en: The Attitude Toward Demons and Evil Spirits
sections.body_en:
We find in the words of the Sages various customs of caution intended to prevent harm from demons and evil spirits; however, over the generations Israel ceased to be careful about them, because those demons and evil spirits were no longer present. We learn this from the custom of being careful about 'pairs' (Pesaḥim 110a): in the days of the Talmud many were careful not to drink cups or eat foods in even numbers, so as not to be harmed by demons. Apparently these demons received their power from the religion of the Magi (of Zoroaster), which believed that there are two powers in the world, good and evil, and those who ate or drank in pairs were harmed by demons and spirits of this idolatry. However, the Sages further stated a general rule (Pesaḥim 110b): "Kol de-kapid – kapdei bahadei, u-de-la kapid – la kapdei bahadei. U-mihu le-meiḥash mibaei." Translation: "Whoever is particular – they are particular with him, and whoever is not particular – they are not particular with him; however, one should be concerned." That is to say, one who is particular to be careful about 'pairs' and was negligent and not careful may be harmed by those demons and evil spirits, while one who is not particular to be careful about 'pairs' is not harmed by those demons and evil spirits. However, ab initio it is better that a person not expose himself to their danger by drinking or eating in pairs, for sometimes they harm even one who is not concerned about them.

The explanation is that the spiritual worlds are composed of different worlds, or in other words, of different dimensions. In every world there are good and beneficial forces as well as evil and harmful ones. In the worlds that tend toward imagination and mysticism, these forces appear as angels, spirits and demons that exert influence for good and for bad, each world according to the type of imaginative consciousness within it. And in the worlds that tend toward the intellect, they appear as good and bad ideas that spread and influence man and humanity, each world according to the conceptions that underlie it.

Every person has his own world of consciousness, and in the world in which his consciousness is found – there he lives. This is what the Sages said: whoever is particular – they are particular with him, and whoever is not particular – they are not particular with him. That is to say, one whose consciousness is in a world of certain spirits and demons, such as those that harm people who drink in pairs, is influenced by them. And one whose consciousness is not there, those demons do not act upon him. Even so, the Sages said that it is proper for him to be concerned about things known to be dangerous. For although his consciousness is far from these demons and spirits, since he lives in a period in which their consciousness is widespread, and he himself is concerned about demons and spirits of a different kind, there is concern that demons and spirits from a neighbouring world of consciousness may also harm him, and therefore it is proper that he beware of their danger.

However, over the course of the generations, most of Israel came to live in the consciousness of intellectual spiritual worlds, in which there is no place for demons and spirits, and even the secrets of the Torah and the rich worlds of imagination are explained by the intellect. Thus the poskim ruled regarding various halakhot that there is no need to be concerned about evil spirits, because they are not present among us. However, people who still give them a place in their worldview, because of their inclination or their upbringing, may be concerned about them according to what their rabbis instruct them.12

notes_en.en:
Regarding the topic of 'pairs', see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 36:6, note 4. Regarding what was said in Nidda 17a, not to eat peeled garlic, onion or egg that have been left overnight, because of the danger of an evil spirit, see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 36:7, note 5, that the Rambam, most Rishonim and the Shulḥan Arukh did not mention this, for already in their time they ruled that there is no need to be concerned about it, since it was not common for this evil spirit to cause harm. So too there, 36:7, note 6, regarding drinking water at the 'hour of the tekufa' (the turn of the season). And even regarding the evil spirit that rests on the hands in the morning, the Tosafists wrote that it no longer causes harm in their days (Tosafot Yoma 77b, s.v. "Mishum shabbeta"; Peninei Halakha, Tefila 8:3).
The power of the demons, spirits and lilin diminishes, because they are creatures that were not completed, and as time passes the world becomes increasingly rectified, desolate places are settled, more things are clarified, and consequently their power diminishes, and the righteous can nullify them. An example of the diminishing of the power of demons we learned in the Talmud (Pesaḥim 112b): "It was taught: A person should not go out alone at night, neither on the nights of Wednesdays nor on the nights of Shabbatot, because Agrat bat Maḥlat, she and eighteen myriads of angels of destruction, go out, and each and every one has permission to destroy on its own." The Gemara explains that at first she was present every night; once "she met Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa. She said to him: Had they not proclaimed concerning you in Heaven, 'Beware of Ḥanina and his Torah', I would have endangered you. He said to her: If I am esteemed in Heaven, I decree upon you that you shall never pass through a settled area. She said to him: I beg of you, leave me a little room. He left her the nights of Shabbatot and the nights of Wednesdays. And again, once she met Abaye. She said to him: Had they not proclaimed concerning you in Heaven, 'Beware of Naḥmani and his Torah', I would have endangered you. He said to her: If I am esteemed in Heaven, I decree upon you that you shall never pass through a settled area." Yet they would still sometimes enter a settled area to retrieve 'horses' that they had lost. End of quote. And although the demons have diminished in their appearance in the world, they still remain within the soul of man as problems that have not been resolved. For more on this see the next section. (And see also above, 19:14, on the diminishing of the powers of sorcery.)

sections.body_en:
Ab initio it is better to educate not to be concerned about demons and evil spirits, just as the Rambam and many of the poskim ignored the prohibitions connected to the danger of demons and evil spirits. This is because the choice not to relate to demons and spirits and not to grant them value nullifies their influence. For they are deficient creatures that did not come to realisation, and unless a person grants them a place in his consciousness, they cannot exert upon him an influence of any weight that needs to be taken into account. Along these lines, my teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook ztz"l used to say that the Rambam did not write anywhere that there are no demons; rather, he decided to ignore them, because his educational-halakhic position was that involvement "in obscure and mystical matters is a danger to the great general public. Therefore the Rambam saw it as a duty to omit them, from the standpoint of the education of all Israel" (Siḥot Ha-Ratziya, Bereshit, pp. 295-297; 310-312). Consequently, even in halakha the Rambam could ignore the danger of demons, for we have already learned that when one is not concerned about the danger of evil spirits and demons, there is no harm from them.13

The more the world develops and further clarifications are made, and the more education exerts a positive influence, the more the influence of harmful demons and spirits diminishes. As Rabbi Yosef Ḥayim of Baghdad wrote more than a hundred years ago: "In our time the power of the Sitra Aḥra has weakened, as you can see that in our time the activity of the spirits and demons that roam the world has diminished, and there has not remained of this matter, of what there was in the time of the early generations, even one part in a thousand. And all this is because of the weakness of the Sitra Aḥra and the diminution of the kelipot, for the one depends on the other, as is known" (Rav Pe'alim, part II, Sod Yesharim 9). On this basis he wrote that all the warnings stated in the Talmud out of concern for demons and evil spirits, such as that a woman should not pass between two men or a man between two women, "were said only in ancient times, when demons and harmful beings were very common, and there were species of different kinds. Now the Sitra Aḥra has weakened, and these too have diminished, and only ab initio it is good to be concerned and careful about this" (Ben Yehoyada, Pesaḥim 111a).

So too in practice, many of the great Torah authorities of recent generations did not relate at all to the warnings stemming from the danger of demons and spirits, and from this their students understood that there is no need to be concerned about them at all. All the more so is this the case in the Land of Israel, "a land which the Lord your God cares for; the eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it" (Devarim 11:12), where the good and the bad in it come from the Lord with more revealed providence, without the intervention of harmful beings.

However, there are customs of caution against an evil spirit that are observed even today because they have an additional reason, such as the concern about drinking water at night from a river lest leeches swarm in it (Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 36:7, note 7), and such as the warning to maintain cleanliness (ibid. 36:8). And sometimes people continue to observe the custom of caution not because of concern about danger but out of respect for the earlier generations who practised it (our master Rav Kook, Responsa Ezrat Kohen 7).14

notes_en.en: So too we learned in Nedarim (32a): "Rabbi said: Whoever practises divination – divination comes upon him … because of measure for measure. Ahava son of Rabbi Zeira taught: Any person who does not practise divination is brought into an enclosure that even the ministering angels cannot enter." Rashi: "Whoever practises divination – that is, who pursues diviners. Divination comes upon him – divinations pursue him, for whoever is particular, they are particular with him." (The prohibition of 'niḥush' (divination) is explained above, 24:3.) One can learn from this that whoever ignores demons and spirits is not harmed by them. And if he ignored them out of faith in the Lord, he merits entering an enclosure that even the ministering angels do not enter. Therefore it is better not to encourage concern about the dangers of demons, but rather to educate to live in the consciousness of an intellectual world, in which the influence of a person's choice is more understandable.

Sometimes a custom whose basis is concern about an evil spirit is observed meticulously because it also has additional reasons. For example, washing the hands three times in the morning: even one who is not concerned about this evil spirit observes it in order to purify himself from the impurity of sleep at night, which is one sixtieth of death; see Peninei Halakha, Tefila 8:3-4.
In general, because of the holiness of the Land of Israel there were always fewer demons in it; thus we find that in the Babylonian Talmud demons are mentioned at length, while in the Yerushalmi only a little and briefly (Maharatz Ḥayot, Mevo Ha-talmud, chapter 31). Along these lines it is cited in the Zohar that the 'Sitra Aḥra' and the forces of impurity have no control in the Land of Israel (Zohar II 140b; III 72b; and the commentary Or Yakar by the Ramak there; and also Zohar I 75b; II 130a). So too Pri Etz Ḥayim wrote in the second introduction: "Even the Angel of Death in the Land of Israel is a good angel, only it clothes itself in judgement and cruelty." And so too in the book Tuv Ha-aretz 3:1; Ḥesed Le-Avraham, Ma'ayan 3:2; Ma'ayan 7:15. And in Ben Yehoyada on Pesaḥim 109b: "… the Sitra Aḥra – its power has weakened, and it was first nullified in the Land of Israel because of its holiness, and afterwards it was nullified in Babylonia too." So too wrote Responsa Ezrat Kohen 6-7, that in the Land of Israel there is not so much room for concern about segula-related (supernatural) dangers.
